articles.text: Despite some rain the weekend of March 11 and 12, more than 500 shoppers attended this year’s Treasures Sale at Piedmont Community Church. The annual sale of thousands of donated goods raised $26,000 for the church’s Youth Mission Trip during Spring Break in which they will build 15 homes outside Tijuana, Mexico. The sale helps pay for building supplies and material plus the food needed for the 195 youth who have signed up to spend the week of April 10-14 building homes for impoverished families in Mexico. Considered a rite of passage for Piedmont teens, the tradition dates back 24 years, during which time more than 350 homes have been built. For most families, it is their first dwelling with a front door and a door lock. The Treasures Sale drew a huge crowd of pickers, deal hunters, antiquers and collectors even before the doors opened at 9:00 a.m. Youth Pastor Scott Kail, who will lead the trip to Mexico this year, estimated that 150 people were lined up waiting to get in and begin bargain hunting. More than 50 volunteers were on hand to help over the weekend, and in the preceding weeks to collect and display all donations. Volunteers put up portable canopies in the courtyard to shelter Youth Pastor Scott Kail thanks volunteers while gathered in the church kitchen for final instructions.

articles.text: The first reference to Eskimo-Intuit peoples having multiple, nuanced words for snow was in the introduction to anthropologist/linguist Franz Boas’ Handbook of American Indian Languages published in 1911. He wrote it after studying the Intuit people of Baffin Island and posited that the structure of language (sound, grammar, vocabulary, etc.) shapes a speaker’s view of the world. But now consider the limitations of our language, the absence of descriptors when we attempt to understand and conceptualize what we refer to as the universe, a word that is understood but also accepted for its expansive vagueness. When an event takes place, astronomers search for language to frame and explain what it is that has been discovered. They need more than 100 words for snow, so to speak. Recently, scientists announced that at last they had captured an image of a stellar phenomenon that up until now had only been theoretical: a black hole. It is something better described as a cosmic abyss, one so deep and dense not even light can escape it. Before now, black holes in space were the stuff of imagination, the geography of writers and artists mining the forgiving realm of science fiction or expressed as computer model algorithms. Now, suddenly, black holes have been revealed as a concrete image of a lopsided ring of red and yellow light, a donut hole of sorts, surrounded by interstellar gas and dust, delineating a redeyed portal into which all matter is pulled, including light. One such eye has been discovered deep in the center of a galaxy known as Messier 87 (M87), some 55 million light-years from earth (in one year, light can travel some 6 trillion miles), meaning the distances in play are beyond extraordinary. To capture the image of M87, 200 astronomers aimed an intercontinental collection of nine mountain top telescopes, called Event Horizon, at the galaxy Virgo, home to M87, a black hole several billion times more massive than our sun. articles.text: Dr. Jonathan C. Augustine is both a pastor in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and a professor of law. In his recent book Called to Reconciliation: How the Church Can Model Justice, Diversity and Inclusion, he notes that it important for us to respect both “the kingdom to come,” the promise of life beyond this life, as well as “the kingdom at hand,” the work God is doing in the here and now. One of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church’s primary commitments to the “kingdom at hand” is our support for, and participation in, the ongoing work of Oakland Ceasefire. I wrote this after spending a day with the leaders of Ceasefire Oakland. On Wednesday, March 8, I was at St. Columba’s Church in North Oakland for the annual Oakland Ceasefire Partnership Retreat. Gathered were service providers, planners, police, clergy, representatives of the elected officials and community members that have made Ceasefire work in Oakland for the last decade. The cover of the notebooks we were given read “Programs don’t change people, relationships do.” At the meeting we recognized that after reducing the number of homicides in Oakland to 67 in 2018 and 75 in 2019, the COVID years have brought a return to annual homicide rates of over 100. We discussed the reasons for this rise while affirming that there is still strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of Ceasefire’s evidence-driven, community-based, relationship building approach to gun violence reduction. At the retreat we reiterated our commitment to keeping people alive and out of jail and reviewed the three central goals of Ceasefire: 1. Reduce shootings 2. Reduce recidivism 3. Build trust between the community and the police During the presentation lifting up the principles of the Ceasefire philosophy I took a picture of a slide titled “Specificity & Intensity.” The slide read. Oakland Ceasefire is a strategy to reduce gun violence in the near term (6, 12, 18 months) and focuses intensive interventions specifically on the largest drivers of violence including: • Retaliatory shootings • Very high risk individuals
articles.title: Ceasefire Oakland strives for reduction in gun violence

articles.text: Silver Buffalo Award to be presented at National Annual Meeting on May 31 The Silver Buffalo Award recognizes adult leaders who have provided distinguished service to youth at a national level. It is the highest award that the National Council BSA (Scouts) can present to its volunteers. Bob Coleman, a recipient of the Silver Buffalo this year, will be recognized at the National Annual Meeting in Atlanta on May 31. He is only the second Piedmont Scouter to receive the award. Wes Smith, also a former Piedmont Council president, was given the award in 2019. “The key reason I’m so committed to Scouting,” said Coleman, “is that the Scouting program for youth is the only one organized around teaching the qualities of leadership to young people. You don’t get that with any other organization. What is leadership? Leadership is a 15-year-old patrol leader at 1 p.m. on a campout weekend trying to get a bunch of wild 11 and 12-year olds to clean up the campsite. That’s leadership, and everyone has to do it. America needs more and better leaders.” Bob has deep roots with Scouting. He is one of three generations of Eagles, including himself, his father, James, and his son, Scott. His father’s adventures in Hungary at the 1933 World Jamboree have served as a family marker ever since. James became penpals with an Austrian Jewish Scout named Jacob. After a few years of corresponding, Jacob confided that his parents wanted him to immigrate to the United States but that he would need a work sponsor. Could James help? Well, James and his father searched and searched and were finally able to cable Jacob with the good news. One day later, this chilling cable came back. “Thank you for all your work to find a work sponsor for Jacob, but you are too late by a day!” James never heard from Jacob again. From this experience was born in James and later his entire family an abiding sense of urgency to get things done, something that carries on to this day. Asked about his proudest moment in Scouting, Bob said, “Participating in the vote to allow gay youth into the program. I wondered at the time, why our own Congress couldn’t work things on such a mature basis. We disagreed, we spoke together, we voted and we moved on, together.” After graduating from Wesleyan College and Harvard Business School, and after a decorated The animals cost up to $600, an impossible sum for a poor family. Some years ago Bob instituted an “animal-back guarantee” program whereby if an animal dies, for any reason, while in the care of the Fondouk, the Fondouk will arrange to find a replacement for that animal through discounted prices from animal brokers, favorable loans directly from the Fondouk or outright gifts. Bob visits Fez every year, and says it is rare when he doesn’t accompany the Fondouk’s local director into a souk to find a replacement animal. The hospital is administered by the Massachusetts SPCA. Their new director just finished a three-year surgical internship at Purdue University and is the first U.S. Board certified equine surgeon on the African continent. Bob has always made a connection between his other philanthropic work and Scouts. Bob’s church, Piedmont Community Church, was a chartering organization for Piedmont Scouts more than 100 years ago. Piedmont Language School was brought into the Council as a Learning for Life crew. In the early 2000s, as a member of the Piedmont Council Executive Board, he led a highly successful campaign to increase the council’s Endowment Fund. In only a few years it became one of the largest such funds in Piedmont and helped put Piedmont on the map of the national organization. Bob’s son, Scott, worked for a time in Geneva, Switzerland, with the World Scout Foundation and was part of the first committee to set up the rules for the Messengers of Peace program. Subsequently, Bob became a substantial supporter of Scouting in Morocco. Just last year, a dedication was held in Fez for the completion of an animal stable to be managed by the Fondouk. The half million dollar project was funded by a generous gift from the World Scout Foundation and significant contributions from the mayor of Fez and the local provincial governor. There was active local Scout participation throughout the project and continues today with local Scouts actually mucking our stalls and assisting with the feeding of the animals. The stable also has a dedicated Scout meeting room. “Never being too late by a day” is the driving force behind Bob’s commitment to Scouting. There is much to be accomplished. It must never be too late to get things done. Former Piedmont Scout Council president Bob Coleman will be presented with Scouting’s highest national award, the Silver Buffalo Award, in Atlanta on May 31. career with the Navy in Vietnam, Bob entered the world of brokerage and wealth management, first with Goldman Sachs and culminating with Merrill Lynch. Bob was listed by Barrons as the 8th top broker in America at a time when he and his team managed $3 Billion in assets. A close relationship with his clients afforded him the ability to help assist in their philanthropic efforts. Bob is also an active member of the Messengers of Peace Committee and an enthusiastic promoter of its mission. Bob is most likely the only Moroccan Sharif folks in Piedmont will meet. This honorific stems from the Coleman family’s 96 years of work as founders of the American Fondouk Animal Hospital in Fez, Morocco. The hospital provides free veterinary treatment of any kind to working animals in Fez, a city of two million people. It is the largest and best equipped animal hospital in Africa, and all veterinary treatment is paid for entirely by American donations. At any one time they routinely have up to 45 horses, donkeys or mules hospitalized for periods of up to one month. These hard-working animals rent out for $3 per day – the entire income for that animal’s human family for the day. Without that income, the family’s alternative would be starvation. The mayor of Fez once observed to Bob that the average poor household in Fez may have five to eight people residing in it. Treating 6 or 7,000 animals per year, that means that the presence of the Fondouk in Fez may keep upwards of 30,000 people from starving each year. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Part 5 in a series Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Lake Merritt Institute Each month, thousands of pounds of trash accumulate in Lake Merritt. Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep the lake’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the shores of Lake Merritt, and usually work for between two and three hours during a shift. Training is provided, as are gloves, trash bags, barrels, nets, directions, and other materials. Cleanups are held five times a week during the school year and 3-4 times a week in the summer. Visit lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-you-can-help to learn more and sign up. Piedmont Branch Library • Treasurer. The Friends of the Piedmont Avenue Library are looking for a treasurer. An ideal volunteer for this role would have knowledge of accounting and recordkeeping, providing oversight of Friends of PAL finances, taking part in board meetings and presenting financial reports to the library’s board. This volunteer would also pay bills, record bank account activity and analyze cash flow, collect and disburse funds, and prepare data for state and federal filing, and work with the library’s fundraising committee to project cash needs and sources. To apply, email contact@ friendsofpal.org with information about your interest and a resume, if available. • Social media coordinator. The Piedmont Avenue Library is also looking for a social media coordinator. This volunteer would manage digital content for FPAL across their social media channels (Facebook, Instagram, Twitter), the library’s website, and the library’s monthly newsletter. The library’s social media channel would be updated on a weekly basis with fun, uplifting content, to make sure that the community stays up-to-date about the latest happenings at the library. Harbor House Harbor House is a nonprofit Christian community development organization in Oakland which has provided a safe place for opportunities, resources, and relationships for children, teens, and families for five decades. Volunteer opportunities include virtual tutoring, food distribution, after-school program teachers, and facility maintenance (gardening and handiwork). To apply or learn more, contact the volunteer coordinator at nicole@hhministries.org or fill out an application at bit.ly/3YBzu16. pages.text: Wednesday, March 15, 2023 3 Bob Coleman earns Scouting’s highest award Silver Buffalo Award to be presented at National Annual Meeting on May 31 The Silver Buffalo Award recognizes adult leaders who have provided distinguished service to youth at a national level. It is the highest award that the National Council BSA (Scouts) can present to its volunteers. Bob Coleman, a recipient of the Silver Buffalo this year, will be recognized at the National Annual Meeting in Atlanta on May 31. He is only the second Piedmont Scouter to receive the award. Wes Smith, also a former Piedmont Council president, was given the award in 2019. “The key reason I’m so committed to Scouting,” said Coleman, “is that the Scouting program for youth is the only one organized around teaching the qualities of leadership to young people. You don’t get that with any other organization. What is leadership? Leadership is a 15-year-old patrol leader at 1 p.m. on a campout weekend trying to get a bunch of wild 11 and 12-year olds to clean up the campsite. That’s leadership, and everyone has to do it. America needs more and better leaders.” Bob has deep roots with Scouting. He is one of three generations of Eagles, including himself, his father, James, and his son, Scott. His father’s adventures in Hungary at the 1933 World Jamboree have served as a family marker ever since. James became penpals with an Austrian Jewish Scout named Jacob. After a few years of corresponding, Jacob confided that his parents wanted him to immigrate to the United States but that he would need a work sponsor. Could James help? Well, James and his father searched and searched and were finally able to cable Jacob with the good news. One day later, this chilling cable came back. “Thank you for all your work to find a work sponsor for Jacob, but you are too late by a day!” James never heard from Jacob again. From this experience was born in James and later his entire family an abiding sense of urgency to get things done, something that carries on to this day. Asked about his proudest moment in Scouting, Bob said, “Participating in the vote to allow gay youth into the program. I wondered at the time, why our own Congress couldn’t work things on such a mature basis. We disagreed, we spoke together, we voted and we moved on, together.” After graduating from Wesleyan College and Harvard Business School, and after a decorated The animals cost up to $600, an impossible sum for a poor family. Some years ago Bob instituted an “animal-back guarantee” program whereby if an animal dies, for any reason, while in the care of the Fondouk, the Fondouk will arrange to find a replacement for that animal through discounted prices from animal brokers, favorable loans directly from the Fondouk or outright gifts. Bob visits Fez every year, and says it is rare when he doesn’t accompany the Fondouk’s local director into a souk to find a replacement animal. The hospital is administered by the Massachusetts SPCA. Their new director just finished a three-year surgical internship at Purdue University and is the first U.S. Board certified equine surgeon on the African continent. Bob has always made a connection between his other philanthropic work and Scouts. Bob’s church, Piedmont Community Church, was a chartering organization for Piedmont Scouts more than 100 years ago. Piedmont Language School was brought into the Council as a Learning for Life crew. In the early 2000s, as a member of the Piedmont Council Executive Board, he led a highly successful campaign to increase the council’s Endowment Fund. In only a few years it became one of the largest such funds in Piedmont and helped put Piedmont on the map of the national organization. Bob’s son, Scott, worked for a time in Geneva, Switzerland, with the World Scout Foundation and was part of the first committee to set up the rules for the Messengers of Peace program. Subsequently, Bob became a substantial supporter of Scouting in Morocco. Just last year, a dedication was held in Fez for the completion of an animal stable to be managed by the Fondouk. The half million dollar project was funded by a generous gift from the World Scout Foundation and significant contributions from the mayor of Fez and the local provincial governor. There was active local Scout participation throughout the project and continues today with local Scouts actually mucking our stalls and assisting with the feeding of the animals. The stable also has a dedicated Scout meeting room. “Never being too late by a day” is the driving force behind Bob’s commitment to Scouting. There is much to be accomplished. It must never be too late to get things done. Bob was listed by Barrons as the 8th top broker in America at a time when he and his team managed $3 Billion in assets. A close relationship with his clients afforded him the ability to help assist in their philanthropic efforts. Bob is also an active member of the Messengers of Peace Committee and an enthusiastic promoter of its mission. Bob is most likely the only Moroccan Sharif folks in Piedmont will meet. This honorific stems from the Coleman family’s 96 years of work as founders of the American Fondouk Animal Hospital in Fez, Morocco. The hospital provides free veterinary treatment of any kind to working animals in Fez, a city of two million people. It is the largest and best equipped animal hospital in Africa, and all veterinary treatment is paid for entirely by American donations. At any one time they routinely have up to 45 horses, donkeys or mules hospitalized for periods of up to one month. These hard-working animals rent out for $3 per day – the entire income for that animal’s human family for the day. Without that income, the family’s alternative would be starvation. The mayor of Fez once observed to Bob that the average poor household in Fez may have five to eight people residing in it. Treating 6 or 7,000 animals per year, that means that the presence of the Fondouk in Fez may keep upwards of 30,000 people from starving each year. articles.text: Nominations for this year’s Heritage Trees are due at City Hall by this Friday, March 17. The Heritage Tree program, which began in 2018, helps raise awareness of and appreciation for the city’s urban forest. Each year Piedmont designates up to five trees or groups of trees as Heritage Trees. Winners are selected from a pool of community nominations by members of the Park Commission and Public Works staff. This year’s Heritage Trees will be announced at the April 11 Park Commission meeting and highlighted at the City’s Arbor Day celebration on April 27 at Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue.. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized as part of the Arbor Day program and receive a heritage tree lapel pin. To nominate a Heritage Tree, download the nomination form at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTreeNomination. Return the completed form to Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager by email at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or by mail at 120 Vista Avenue. Please provide the following information: • the species of the tree or group of trees you’d like to see recognized • address or general location • description of the tree • explanation of the aesthetic, educational, or historical qualities that make this tree noteworthy • photo or link to a map showing the location of the tree, if available Trees selected as this year’s Heritage Trees will join 23 others that have received the designation since 2018. Last year’s winners were the Deodar Cedar at the traffic circle at Alta and Scenic Avenues; the Melaleuca at Beach playground on Linda Avenue; the Northern Catalpa street tree at 46 Nace Avenue; and the Autumn Blaze Maples on the 400 block of Wildwood Avenue. An interactive map of the City’s Heritage Trees, with photos and information on each tree, is available on the City’s Heritage Tree program webpage at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTrees. This year’s Arbor Day celebration will take place on April 27 at p.m. at Community Hall (711 Highland Avenue). In addition to recognition of the new Heritage Trees, the event will feature an “Ask an Arborist” booth, food and drink, music from the Piedmont High School jazz band, and a showcase of the trucks and equipment Public Works staff use to keep the city’s trees healthy and thriving. The popular chalk art contest and gratitude trees will return in the week leading up to the festivities. With questions about the Heritage Tree program, please contact Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent by email at nkent@ piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3064.

The trees which fell on Trestle Glen Road and Glen Alpine Road were cleared within hours by Friday. On Tuesday, March 14, police reported in mid-afternoon, “PG&E power lines are down and damaged on Moraga Ave. The power is out in the area and Moraga Ave. is closed between Maxwelton and Highway 13.” As of 6 p.m. last night, PG&E showed that there were power outages in the area at the Piedmont-Oakland border. articles.text: The Piedmont High School Affinity Mentors class invites the Piedmont community, young and old, to an event on Monday, March 20, at the Alan Harvey Theater. The discussion at 7:00 p.m. will provide student perspectives on inclusion versus exclusion and aims to help kids become allies. Students will share their personal experiences with prejudice, discuss the current culture of “othering,” and confront the persistent use of slurs and other forms of microaggression. Student panelists, and speakers along with adult moderators will offer ideas on how the families in our community can be allies to continue to build a culture of belonging in Piedmont. This event welcomes everyone who lives or works in Piedmont and is appropriate for older elementary students and up. The student speakers will be Sohrab Ford, Morgan Hunt, and Stephanie Tsung. articles.text: Elective course was created by English teacher Mercedes Foster Piedmont High School English teacher Mercedes Foster created and implemented a new elective course this year, Film as Literature. The one-semester course looks deeply into film elements. Judging by student engagement and excitement when this reporter came to visit on Friday, March 10, the class is a blockbuster hit. The day’s lesson focused on a narrative device known as a longtake tracking shot. Students were familiar with the war movie 1917 which attempts to have long-takes and as few cuts as possible. “Does anyone know what a long-take tracking shot is?” Foster queried, to which students comfortably offered answers near and far to the mark. Foster explained the long-take tracking shot as one which uses camera movement and one continuous shot without cuts. Longtake tracking shots can follow or depart from certain characters, objects or tropes, which requires film direction to come from multiple angles at timely intervals. The lights came down in the room and the 1927 silent film directed by William A. Wellman, Wings, served as the first example – a pioneer of the “dolly shot” with a moving camera to create action cinematography. Foster challenged her class to keep in mind how heavy and bulky the cameras were at the time, the timing of the actors, and if moving out of the way of the moving camera was done naturally. The class then jumped through the history of film to 1958 for a famous opening long-take tracking shot in A Touch of Evil, directed by Orson Welles. Other examples included the opening Senior Callan Mitchell (left), junior Jonah Dupree and senior Paden Andrews brainstorm ideas for their shot. Mercedes Foster goes over a few details about long-take tracking shots with senior Teagan Haddawy. scenes of Baby Driver (2017) directed by Edgar Wright and the 1992 film The Player, directed by Robert Altman. Foster described the latter as “half expose and half satire of the inner workings of Hollywood.” Junior Jonah Dupree pointed out the circular movement of the camera in The Player, emphasizing the circular, chaotic conversations that were the subject of the shot. After viewing the examples, small groups of students were tasked with mapping out their own long-take tracking shots with specific criteria: at least three recognizable interactions, an over the shoulder angle, a zoom-in close up, and a pause in movement for at least two seconds. Students eagerly brainstormed their plots and plans for direction then scouted out possible sites on campus. “How do you trigger your actor’s actions on time, during these long scenes without cuts?” Foster asked her class. In 2022, Foster pitched the idea of the course to the school board with a detailed curriculum, the course philosophy and sample course content. If a potential course survives the scrutiny of two readings at school board meetings it can be implemented into the school district curriculum. The class’s first assignment this semester had small groups plot, direct and record a silent film. Their second task built on the first as students recorded sound and music to the silent film, using the “Foley” technique or by recording audio and adding music during post-production. On March 15 the class will be filming long-take tracking shots around campus. This Friday the class will write essays about romantic-comedies, or rom-coms, and Foster will treat the class to popcorn during the assessment. Students are not limited to the obvious fits for that genre and are challenged to pick any movie and find a rom-com element no matter how unconventional or obscure. Later in the semester the class will explore Bildungsroman, or a coming-of-age story, chronicling life events that define characters. Senior Paden Andrews decided to take the semester course twice in a row and now serves as a teacher’s assistant for the class. Discussions get lively as these future Tarentinos and Scorseses exude their love of film, prompting Foster to start a wall for future recommended films in the class. “This is a very sharp group; I’ve been blown away with how much my students already know about film. It’s constantly humbling,” said Foster. Teagan Haddawy (left), Ian Shea, and Eden Lorin plan out their long-take tracking shot which will follow a tray of food through the student center with an “extra” ingredient.

articles.text: When the sun sets, the night sky lights up as stars begin to shine above us. Stars range in different sizes and colors, but have you ever looked at a star and wondered how it was formed? Nebulas Star formation begins inside nebulas, which are large clouds of gas and dust. With the help of gravity, the clouds collect and begin to collapse. This collapse creates the core that will become a star. The core is called a protostar and while spinning quickly, heat and pressure goes up. The rising temperature and pressure cause a reaction, which takes us to the next stage of star formation. The Main Sequence The main sequence is the second stage of a star’s lifecycle. At this point, gravity and heat inside the star have balanced. During this phase, stars stop growing or shrinking and begin to shine. What makes stars shine? A reaction takes place inside the star’s core that give it the energy to shine and to stop it from breaking down. The bigger the star, the faster it will use up energy. After using all the energy, the star will move to the next step. The next phase of a star depends on its size. Average Stars When an average sized star runs out of energy it enters the phase called a red giant. During this phase, the star gets bigger and changes in color because of the temperature change. After this stage, the star goes through an explosion called a planetary nebula. As time passes, the outer layers from this explosion will fade away. What is left behind are remains known as white dwarfs. The lifecycle of most average stars will end as white dwarfs. Massive Stars When a massive star runs out of energy, it will first become a super red giant. The size and color changes are more extreme because the star is massive. Next, the super red giant will break down and cause a gigantic explosion, which will lead the star to become a neutron star or a black hole. A regular massive star will end as a neutron star. A neutron star is the core of the star that was left from the explosion. A super massive star will end as a black hole. A black hole is a space that has a strong gravity that can consume other objects. Each star has its own journey, but they all shine above us at some point in time. Stars are different yet in many ways alike. As we continue to explore space, we might get to learn even more about star formation. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Last weekend 34 members from Highlander Robotics traveled to Fresno with their robot, Paddo the Frog, for the FIRST Robotics Competition Central Valley Regional. After finishing 4th of 38 in qualification rounds with a 10-2 record, they went 4-1 during the double elimination playoffs to challenge the first seed alliance captained by former world champion MadTown Robotics from Madera. They lost two straight in the best of three finals to finish second overall. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by high school students. The competition arena is about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall score points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals as well as by balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station.” During regional competitions, teams play up to 12 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners. The highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft two others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoffs. Draft selections are key to success in the playoffs. All teams at the elite level dedicate significant time and personnel to track every robot’s performance in what can be well over 100 qualifying rounds. The Highlanders, which reached division semi-finals at the World Championships in 2022, substantially improved their scouting system in anticipation of Charged Up. In the fall, Monte Vista freshman Jacob Trentini and Millennium High freshman Colin Cameron wrote an iPhone app while at an off-season competition which simplifies the collection of scouting data. They were later joined by PHS freshman Cassie Colby and senior Barry Balasingham. The four expanded Trentini and Cameron’s proof of concept to a cross platform collection system with score prediction and sophisticated analytic tools. At the end of the first day of qualifications, the Highlanders were in third place after nine Software lead Lewy Seiden makes last minute programming changes. Ambassador Jessica Liu and Pit Lead Helena Young staff the Highlander Robotics pit. Pit Crew members Asha Byers and Chloe Kessinger tune up the robot between matches. rounds. They lost one match due to an alliance partner’s malfunction. In their remaining three qualifiers, they dropped to fourth after an agonizingly close loss to the East Palo Alto Churrobots, 82-80. During the draft, the Highlanders became the third seed alliance captain. Their first pick, the fifth-ranked Buchanan Bird Brains from Clovis, secured a solid scoring partner but their second pick, the 36th ranked Breaker Bots from Pacific Grove, left many scratching their heads. “While they were close to the bottom of the rankings, the scouting data indicated they were ideal for defense,” explained team captain Alex Ware. In their first playoff round, the Highlanders suffered a huge upset by the sixth seed alliance when the Bird Brains robot malfunctioned and became disabled 45-seconds into the match. They fought back, however, and the gamble of their second pick paid off when they won four straight to clinch a finals appearance after edging out the second seed alliance captained by the Churrobots, 124-114. In the best-of-three finals, the Highlanders lost in two world record-setting performances, 162- 117 and 165-95, to a powerhouse alliance formed by captain MadTown Robotics from Madera, the Greybots from Atascadero, and the Arborbots from Visalia. MadTown and the Greybots are both former world champions with four titles between them including one they earned together in 2019. The Highlanders gather at the end of a very exciting weekend.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team is back and in action this spring, currently at 2-1 through three matches. It opened the season with a 13-9 win over Monte Vista at Witter Field on Tuesday, March 7, lost narrowly 15-14 to Marin Academy on Thursday, March 9 in San Rafael, and pummeled Moreau Catholic 18-3 in Hayward last Friday, March 10. The Highlanders return with a wealth of talent from last year’s team and are the favorites to win the Western Alameda County Conference. It would be Piedmont’s seventh consecutive league banner. PHS also returns to North Coast Section’s Division 2 as a team-to-watch after playing in Division 1 since winning the Div. 2 title in 2019. It’s worth mentioning that Marin Academy and Monte Vista are Div. 1 teams. “We have a lot of returners, we’re a strong team that’s senior heavy. We’ve already had some strong performances. We beat Monte Vista and they’re a terrific team; it’s a really good way to start the season. Marin Academy is another strong Division 1 team and that was a back-and-forth game [played] in the pouring rain. It’s exactly the type of game we need; we want to be roadready and play against the best,” said PHS coach Alex Yu. Piedmont returns all four team Nathan Fredericks, last year’s leading scorer, is back as a senior. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team is in pursuit of its seventh consecutive WACC title, with eyes on winning the NCS banner. captains from last season: Nathan Fredericks, Soren Dixon, Henry Brayer and Jack Nelson. Other returners include Oliver Shafroth, Curtis Hohener, Rylan Nelson, Andrew McLaughlin, Keita Clear, Cairo Osman, Logan Huh, Bede Levin, Gus von Metzsch, Bailey Cain, and Axel Saldanha. “We have Henry back and he’s been hungry. Every force is deadly in our attack, we’re running offenses that start from behind the net, up top, and from the sides. It’s difficult for a defense to cover every angle of the field,” said Fredericks. “I definitely think we should compete for the [North Coast] D2 title. After last year, I think the continuity on our roster really makes us a No. 1 contender… We’ve all been playing together for the last three years and it feels like we’re in our prime right now. To get there, PHS bashed No. 2 University 3-0 on February 22 in the semifinals, beat No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18, and shut out No. 15 Sacred Heart 2-0 in the first round on February 15. articles.text: Highlanders top NCS opponent Campolindo 4-3 spring. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team will have a new look this spring. After losing eight players to graduation, there will be some new faces in the singles and double lineups. The Highlanders are currently 1-2 after defeating Campolindo 4-3 at home on Wednesday, March 8, and losing to both Berkeley (6-1 on March 2) and Branson (6-0 on March 1). “We lost eight players – about half the team. A good portion of them were starters. We’re a bit stronger at the top and weaker at the bottom,” said coach Jim Landes. PHS has returning starters who earned significant time last season, notably Ethan Pham, Ben Breber, and Monte Imburg. Nick King, Arun Brahma, Brady Colbert, and Graham Alban also saw some action in 2022. “Ethan Pham is playing great. He’s a senior and won his match against Campolindo. Monte is a junior and would probably rather play doubles, but we put him at singles, too,” said Landes. Atop the singles order is a freshman, Lucas Smolko, who Landes considers the best 9th grade varsity member since tennis Mackie McDonald, now playing professionally around the world. Smolko is currently rated as a 3-star recruit by TennisRecruiting.net. “Lucas is our No. 1. He’s been playing since he was very young and is a tournament player. He plays in some national tournaments and is a good No. 1. He’s probably the best freshman I’ve seen on the team in a long time, maybe since McDonald,” said Landes. Despite the loss to Berkeley, Landes thinks his team is capable of competing for the Western Alameda County Conference title. I feel we have a chance to win the league,” said Landes. 4-3 over Campolindo Playing No. 1, Smolko won in singles in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. articles.text: Everything, Everywhere is the big winner And so the 2022 Academy Awards began at the Hollywood Dolby Theater, hosted by Jimmy Kimmel, looking more like the ceremonies of the past. The twotiered venue was filled with the glitterati, with masks and social distancing a thing of the past, as if declaring the pandemic was finally behind us. This year the celebrities entered not on the traditional red carpet, but one the color of champagne, where they paused for brief, sometimes awkward interviews. What struck me almost immediately was the diversity of the Oscars, and clearly the Academy had heard the voiced critique of its homogeneity. As one member of the Oscars stated, the ceremony broke another glass ceiling. This year it pertained to Asian actors who were newly represented and took home seven statues. The Oscar award is the industry celebrating itself, reminding us that films can be an art form, and are testimony to the power of the imagination, collaboration, and storytelling. Unlike in years past, we were reminded that there is an ongoing debate regarding where movies should be viewed – in darkened theaters filled with strangers with a movie on an enormous screen, or in living rooms using streaming platforms such as Netflix, Prime or HBO MAX. Regardless of the outcome (will walk-in theaters become a thing of the past?), find below the results of the Oscar winners. • Best Picture: Everything, Everywhere, All At Once • Best Actor in a Leading Role: Brendan Fraser - The Whale • Best Actress in a Leading Role: Michelle Yeoh – Everything, Everywhere, All At Once • Best Actor in a Supporting Role: Ke Huy Quan – Everything, Everywhere All At Once • Best Actress in a Supporting Role: Jamie Lee Curtis – Everything, Everywhere All At Once • Best Animated Feature Film: Guillermo Del Toro’s – Pinocchio Best Picture: Everything, Everywhere, All At Once Best Animated Feature Film: Guillermo Del Toro’s – Pinocchio Best Actor in a Leading Role: Brendan Fraser - The Whale Best Actress in Leading Role: Michelle Yeoh – Everything, Everywhere, All At Once Best Actor in a Supporting Role: Ke Huy Quan – Everything, Everywhere All At Once Best Actress in a Supporting Role: Jamie Lee Curtis – Everything Everywhere All At Once Best International Feature Film: All Quiet on the Western Front • • • Best Directing: Daniel Kwan and Daniel Sheinert – Everything, Everywhere, All At Once Best Cinematography: James Friend – All Quiet on the Western Front Best Documentary Feature Film: Navalny • • • Best International Feature Film: All Quiet on the Western Front – Germany Best Original Screenplay: Everything, Everywhere, All At Once Best Adapted Screenplay: Women Talking

articles.text: The ongoing Berkeley Symphony & Friends chamber music concert series, now in its 10th year at Piedmont Center for the Arts, continues this Sunday, March 19, at 4 p.m. with a concert entitled Spring Fever. Following Berkeley Symphony’s sold-out chamber performance in February, Spring Fever will feature Astor Piazzolla’s tango classic, The Four Seasons of Buenos Aires. With its echoes of jazz and its intriguing rhythmic meters, it will serve as a prelude to the Symphony’s Symphonic concert at Zellerbach Hall on April 2. “Spring Fever provides audiences with the opportunity to experience Berkeley Symphony in an intimate venue,” said René Mandel, Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director. “This performance will feature a range of delightful, rich music as we celebrate the changing seasons. March 19th also celebrates our 10th anniversary presenting chamber concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts.” The program includes Lili Boulanger’s enchanting D’un matin de printemps (Of a Spring Morning) and Antonin Dvořák’s “Dumky” Piano Trio in A Minor, a richly passionate masterpiece based on Eastern European folk music. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org or by calling the symphony box office at (510) 841-2800.

articles.text: The Sophie Florence Trio will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 17, at 7:30 p.m. Sink back into the mid-20th century, to a night of nostalgia as the Sophie Florence Trio revisits the songs of Ella Fitzgerald, Dina Washington and Patsy Cline. Relive the diverse array of songs that stamped themselves into American culture, like White Rabbit, Summertime, Love Potion Number 9, I Shall be Released, All of Me, House of the Rising Sun, Tennessee Waltz, and many more. The Sophie Florence Trio is headed by vocalist Sophie Florence Prestwich, a young British woman who met Yalies Chuck Jacob ’73, of Brooklyn, NY, and Phil Hirschi ’73, of Seattle, while all were in Queretaro, Mexico. Prestwich is lead singer and plays flute; Phil Hirschi is on guitar and vocals; and Jacob is on upright bass and mandolin. Sophie, from Colchester, England, started playing flute when she was seven and had classical training as a vocalist starting at age 12. She has a fascination with music from the 1950s and ‘60s, and a particular fondness for Patsy Cline, Dinah Washington and Ella Fitzgerald. After studying French and Film at university and spending a year in Paris, she taught English in South America, and then moved to Queretaro, Mexico, where she met her bandmates, Phil and Chuck. A feast of music from the Great American Songbook awaits the audience, especially music from the 1940s to 1960s, Sophie has had classical training, as have both men, who are seasoned musicians who’ve performed in bands since high school. Phil has toured internationally with John McLaughlin and has recorded. All three play a variety of instruments from flute to piano, to bass, to cello, guitar, and mandolin, and will make use of all in this sure-to-be-stunning Piedmont concert. Don’t miss this one-night-only performance at Piedmont Center for the Arts as the trio kicks off their West Coast Tour. Advance tickets are $23 at www.bpt. me/5741445, and $25 tickets will be available at the door. Doors open at 7 pm. articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson COLORFORMS is San Francisco Ballet’s first film-to-stage adaptation in the company’s 90-year history. San Francisco Ballet will show Myles Thatcher’s COLORFORMS, the company’s first film-to-stage adaptation, now through Sunday, March 19. Thatcher’s creation first debuted as a dance film in San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season, when arts venues were shuttered due to the COVID pandemic. Vibrant in staging and hue, COLORFORMS will open with Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight (2004) and closes with William Forsythe’s Blake Works I (2016), set to seven songs from James Blake’s album The Colour in Anything. “I’m so grateful to have the opportunity to work with these dancers who are not only physically talented, but also intelligent and capable and generous with their spirit, movement, and time,” said Thatcher. “It’s incredible to work with people who you know and trust, and who know you. Making COLORFORMS is the dream.” The production is staged by Ayman Harper, with costume design by Dorothee Merg and choreographer William Forsythe. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling the box office at 415-865- 2000. Showtimes vary and all performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco.

articles.text: Registration required, weather permitting San Francisco Opera is taking opera outside with Boheme Out of the Box. Now through April 2, at select outdoor locations throughout the Bay Area, audiences will be able to hear an abridged version of Giacomo Puccini’s La Bohème. Puccini’s classic was the very first opera to be presented by the San Francisco Opera 100 years ago. His well-known story of love and art will be condensed to one hour and performed in South San Francisco, Los Gatos and Dublin. Boheme Out of the Box is directed by Jose Maria Condemi, is sung in Italian but with English dialogue. The opera will be performed by a rotating panel of guest artists and San Francisco Opera’s Adler Fellows. All performances include piano accompaniment. From Friday through Sunday, March 17-19, the opera will be performed free in South San Francisco. It will be performed the following weekend in Los Gatos and then Dublin. Each performance will offer a unique setting and set design. As an added bonus for audiences, SF Opera is providing an in-depth lecture with scholars one hour in advance of Friday and Saturday performances. Register online at https:// w w w.sfopera.com /seasons/ opera-out-of-the-box/ for details of locations and times of performances. Although performances are free, registration is on a first come, first served basis. All performances are based upon clear weather. articles.text: Production by South African artist William Kentridge Cal Performances presents the U.S. premiere of South African visual artist William Kentridge’s newest production, SIBYL, this weekend, Friday through Sunday, March 17-19, at Zellerbach Auditorium on the UC Berkeley campus. articles.text: Homeward Bound: The It’s an interesting experience to approach a film with one set of expectations and realize, as the story evolves, that it is something else entirely. That’s the case with Mr. Holmes. Going in I assumed that the setting would be London, during those nascent years of the 20th century, not long after the end of WWI. Mr. Holmes is at the top of his deductive game and often takes intricate cases with subtle clues to be cleverly unraveled. Buttressing my assumption is the fact that Ian McKellen, a gifted character actor, is portraying Holmes, minus the deerstalker cap and oversized Meerschaum pipe, but in all ways a perfectly cast Holmes. But Mr. Holmes is a decidedly different movie. Based on the novel A Slight Trick of the Mind, by Mitch Cullin, the narrative is set in 1947. Sherlock Holmes, now in his 90s, is living on his bucolic Sussex farm. He has been retired for some 30 years and has used this time to raise bees and study botany. He lives a solitary life, with the exception of his housekeeper, Mrs. Munro (Laura Linney), and her precocious 10-yearold son, Roger (Milo Parker). As is soon made evident, Mr. Holmes is a penetrating character study of a man once renowned, thanks to the embellished writings of his friend and case collaborator, Dr. John H. Watson, who wrote what Holmes refers to as “penny dreadfuls” (dime store novels in the U.S.) about their exploits. He has retreated from his former life and is now confronted with the harsh realities of aging – his once keen mind going sideways, his powers of observation, always the fulcrum of his detection, growing increasingly elusive. Holmes is gradually becoming a man who has outlived the person he once cherished: his former self. His daily frustration with his decline, compounded by regret for certain choices from his past, have made him taciturn and even a bit desperate. At one point, his face folding in emotional pain, he acknowledges, “I have been alone all of my life.” There is one seemingly minor case offered up through flashbacks, relevant because it causes Holmes such pain that its conclusion results in his retirement. What he is intent on recalling are the events surrounding his profound disillusionment, but he remembers only that the year was 1919 and it involved a recently married woman (Hattie Morahan) who was enamored with learning to play the glass harmonica. Against her husband’s wishes. Holmes is hired to follow her and discover how she is paying for her lessons. What he can’t sort out is what occurred that caused him to leave his flourishing practice and move to Sussex from London where he has remained for 30 years. With the encouragement of Roger, who has clandestinely read the initial pages, Holmes tries to write down the details of the case, hoping to puzzle out its denouement. Meanwhile, he is also in search of a restorative herb that will revitalize his mind as well as his body, He even makes a journey to Hiroshima, Japan, but to no avail. What makes Mr. Holmes worthwhile is the exceptional performance of Ian McKellen. He is, in every respect, Sherlock Holmes: in the backstory we see a face that is a study in incisive intelligence and vitality, his style incomparable. It’s only later that he falls into a kind of helpless sadness and longs for what once was and no longer is. McKellen is, in a word, remarkable in both roles. It is based on the 1960 Sheila Burnford children’s story about three animals – Shadow (Don Ameche), a wise old Golden Retriever; Chance (Michael J. As Disney long ago learned, kids find giving human voices to animals completely acceptable, even when animation is blended with live action characters. articles.text: Dr. Stephen Main, the talented Music Director of Piedmont Community Church for 30 years, sat down for a recent conversation with the Piedmont Post about his background as an organist, pianist, choral director, composer of liturgical music, and as a film score composer. “Having been born and raised in New York City,” said Main, “my father, Tom Main, was always very supportive of my path. He played trombone professionally with Si Zentner’s jazz band in the 1960s, so music has been in my blood from the start.” Main attended Choate Rosemary Hall, a boarding school in Connecticut, where choir students sang at St. Thomas Church in Midtown Manhattan. “I discovered then how much I love choral music,” he said, “and I also got introduced to the pipe organ. It was my first great love. One of my degrees is in organ performance.” Main went on to study in college at Oberlin Conservatory in Ohio, with a double major in music and Religious Philosophy. “My father’s emphasis on liberal arts was wise — I got an M.A. and Ph.D. in Religious Philosophy at the University of Chicago,” he said. I met a man at the law school there who worked summers in San Francisco, and I did a year of doctoral research at Stanford. I got my job at Piedmont Community Church around this time, as well.” In 2004, wanting to expand his music career, Main started composing film scores. He has done work for films like “Mr. Marceau” (2010), “All Alone” (2011), “After the Wizard” (2011), “A Family of Clowns” (2013), and for the TV sitcom “Husbands” (2011-2013). “All church musicians work situationally,” Main explained. “You have three oboe players and a soprano who sings slightly flat available on a Sunday, so you write on the fly for them. Film music is a lot like church music. It’s not a concert; the music is only there to service some larger production, but the whole doesn’t work as well without the music.” Main still travels back and forth from the Bay to Los Angeles every two to three months. Ten years ago he would stay for a week every month. “At first, I couldn’t afford to say no to anything — an ad jingle, or something someone else could have done better, like writing for a rock ‘n’ roll band. Now I’m lucky I can explore my specialty: orchestral, choral, keyboard sounds.” Main intends to continue his work at Piedmont Community Church for the foreseeable future. Dr. Stephen Main is Music Director of Piedmont Community Church. He emphasized that the connection offered by composing and conducting for live performance, usually absent in film work, drew him to music to begin with. “One day I might get hit by a beer truck and some dynamic new musician will turn the place around, but for now people assume that that’s how the music has to sound. I’ve been really lucky,” he said. “Piedmonters not only love music deeply, but understand that orchestras and choirs need a scale of funding that writing and painting don’t. After 30 years, there’s a lot of gut-trust with it – the willingness to say, ‘Yes, let’s try this new cockamamie thing that Steve’s come up with.” For example, the church’s annual Christmas concert started in 2011 with a cantata that Main wrote, inspired by a woman’s reaction to a choir and organ piece of his. “She asked: ‘If you knew you had the orchestra and choir from the get-go, rather than starting with a piano piece, how would you write differently?’ I knew I’d write cinematically, shaping more of a story atmosphere with the music.” Although Main is somewhat relieved to currently have the least-busy work docket he’s had in four years, he is still “writing frantically” for a choir and orchestra project in the works for the church called “The Image,” which will premier on June 4. Instead of a standard sermon that day, the concert will take over. “The piece is a narrative, a cinematic, almost operatic history of Western religion,” he said. “The commissioner is keeping a very low profile about it,” said Main, “but he gave me a tall order. Initially I was to pick the words from American poets like Emerson and Whitman, but I didn’t want to twist them out of context — so we agreed I’d write the verses too. It’s an incredibly ambitious project; I hope everyone can mark their calendars.”
articles.title: Stephen Main: PCC music director, film composer

articles.text: Imagine you’re an ordinary soul minding your own business, when a couple of thugs snatch you, drive you to an isolated house, accuse you of being a spy and then try to finish you off by pouring liquor down your throat and stuffing you behind the wheel of a sports car they send off down a perilously winding mountain road. Whew! Now imagine this is all great fun, which it is, because it’s the opening gambit of the classic Alfred Hitchcock thriller, North by Northwest, which entertained an enthusiastic crowd at the third gathering of the Piedmont’s new movie group, the Second Thursday Flix Fest. At the end of the showing last week, one audience member shouted out, “That was great!” The film group meets at the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with the film beginning at 10:30 a.m. The event is free and open to those 18 and older. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Registration with the PRD is required at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Audience members may bring snacks or lunch. Bob Hall introduced the 1959 film, noting that Hitchcock made it after Vertigo, which was recently voted the best movie of all time by a panel of international critics. Vertigo, however, was a “dark” film, with an unhappy ending, and Hitchcock wanted to follow it with something light, just for fun, so he and his screenwriter, Ernest Lehmann (who also wrote Psycho) concocted this enjoyably preposterous chase film. Cary Grant, in his fourth collaboration with the director, dashes all over the U.S. pursued both by bad guys, headed by actor James Mason, and by the police, who think he’s a murderer. Any upside? Grant gets to meet and romance Eva Marie Saint. Not bad. There’s also Bernard Hermann’s stirring musical score. And then there’s the experience of two classic movie sequences: (1) when a crop duster tries to machine-gun our hero in a corn field, and (2) when Grant and Saint, pursued by armed spies, scramble across the four giant presidential faces carved into the Mount Rushmore monument. The Second Thursday Flix Fest meets again at the Center for the Arts on April 13. The movie will be an award-winning drama dealing with social issues that will be announced to the group in April. articles.text: To kick off Earth Month on April 1, a Bay Area event called the Regenerative Gala will promote the concepts of ethical consumerism and fashion and art as a vehicle for change. The event’s fashion show rejects so-called “fast fashion” which produces clothes in sweatshops, often made from petroleum-based synthetic fabrics. Joelle Provost, a low-impact painter whose works will be featured, said the focus is on natural fabrics produced on farms avoiding pesticides, rejuvenating the soil, and paying a living wage. “A lot of small brands are saying, let’s source our textiles from the farmers so that we know that the ecosystems are being supported on those small farms,” Provost explained. “It’s all about small-batch fabrics.” The gala takes place on Saturday, April 1, at 6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, in Piedmont. Tickets are $150–$300 and available online at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/410109317007. An art auction will feature works promoting a healthy environment and the fight against climate change. To explore the auction and register to bid remotely, go to https://givebutter.com/c/ GnyZu0/auction. Julian Adon Alexander, The Regenerative Gala will feature a runway with models wearing fashions made of natural fabrics produced on farms. another featured artist, will offer paintings raising awareness about the lack of green space in urban neighborhoods of color. “I just think exposure to new ideas is really the point of art,” Alexander noted. “I don’t think it necessarily solves problems, it just introduces something into somebody’s mind.” Food & wine The Gala will feature a chef that works closely with local USDA organic farmers and is committed to minimal packaging. Also featured are wines from a permaculture vineyard in Sonoma County. The Gala will emphasize low-waste, local products to inspire people to use their lifestyle and purchasing power to live in harmony with the earth rather than plunder its natural resources. Proceeds will benefit the Agrarian Trust, a nonprofit supporting land access for the next generation of farmers.

articles.text: • Make sure your recyclables are empty, clean, dry The City of Piedmont has “single stream” recycling where all recyclable materials are put into one bin and eventually separated at a facility in Richmond. If recyclable materials haven’t been rinsed or cleaned out ahead of time, it can cause a mess. Paper is especially vulnerable to grease and moisture. One half-full soda can or greasy takeout container can contaminate the other recyclables in the bin, turning them into trash. • Don’t be an “aspirational” recycler Have you ever put an item in the recycling bin because you thought it should be recyclable? This phenomenon is known as aspirational recycling or “wishcycling.” Such materials include single-use utensils and straws, plastic bags, chip bags, and waxed cartons. Often, wishcycling contaminates recyclables and causes whole batches of recyclable loads to be thrown away. Remember: When in doubt, throw it out. • Don’t include e-waste E-waste can be recycled, but it doesn’t belong in the blue bin. Batteries can be dropped off at the Fire Department or can be placed in a sealed zip-lock plastic bag on top of your blue recycling cart on your regular collection day. For other e-waste items, call Republic Services at 800-320-8077 to schedule a curbside pickup. • If it’s smaller than a credit card, it belongs in the trash Small items like clothing tags, bottle caps, straws, and scraps of paper can clog machinery and are unlikely to be recycled. Recycling loads are delivered to Richmond where they are unloaded and put on conveyor belts for mechanical removal of aluminum cans, plastics and glass. The remaining materials are hand-sorted to recover cardboard and other reusable material as possible. • Don’t bag your recyclables Plastic bags can clog recycling equipment, which may lead sorting facilities to throw away your bagged recyclables. By omitting the bag, you’re creating less waste. • Reduce and reuse before you recycle Did you know that the three R’s are in that order for a reason? Recycling should be a last resort, after reducing and reusing. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Dr. Daniel Sperling, the Distinguished Blue Planet Prize Professor of Civil Engineering and Environmental Science and Policy and founding Director of the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California in Davis, was the guest speaker on March 1 in Piedmont. His discussion was sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Dr. Sperling described renewable electricity generation and EV usage as the #1 and #2 solutions to climate damage. The shift to EVs is already underway with EVs representing 13% of passenger car sales worldwide in 2022. China and the E.U. lead EV passenger sales with approximately 54% and 29% of global unit sales respectively. The U.S. is a distant 3rd place with less than 12% of passenger EV unit sales. Among U.S. states, California is a front-runner in the transition to EVs. Currently, 20% of California’s passenger car sales are EVs – good news for local air quality and public health. Dr. Sperling has kept California in the vanguard of climate leadership in the transportation sector. For the past 16 years, he has held the Transportation seat on the California Air Resources Board (CARB), which adopted its first EV rules in 1990. EV adoption is scheduled to accelerate in California with CARB regulations mandating that EVs reach 33% of passenger car sales by 2026, 66% by 2030 and 100% by 2035. New buses will have to be 100% ZEV (Zero-Emission Vehicles) by 2029 and even new long-haul trucks will be ZEV by 2035. Enabling this rapid transition has been the precipitous decline in battery prices which have decreased 90% in real dollars, from approximately $1,200/ kWh in 2010 to roughly $100/ kWh today. Dr. Sperling shared some mild uncertainties about the pace of EV adoption including fluctuations in battery costs, lags in domestic battery materials supplies, processing, and manufacturing, and slower development of public charging infrastructure, especially to support long-haul road transportation. He is convinced by historical precedents that public and private investment will generate market solutions to surmount these hurdles. In addition to EVs, Dr. Sperling discussed the benefits of, and use-case scenarios for, hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles. He said that hydrogen fuel cells are likely to be important for larger vehicles such as buses and long-haul transportation needs, or for people living in very cold climates who have very long daily commutes. Dr. Sperling closed the session by taking questions from the audience. When asked about housing policy and public transit as means of reducing vehicle-miles-traveled, Dr. Sperling emphasized that reducing vehicle use is a winning strategy that is worthy of public investment. To illustrate this point, he cited the example of his home city of Davis where urban planners and city leaders gradually built a network of safe bike paths widely used by riders of all ages. He said that bikes now account for 30-40% of work trips in Davis. In addition to developing safe biking infrastructure, especially to connect the “last mile” of homes and businesses to public transit, he sees shared, autonomous transportation-on-demand as a promising solution for reducing vehicle-use and for providing convenient and affordable public transportation using larger cars or vans. He notes 3 companies who are currently testing this technology on a limited basis in the Bay Area. Additional question topics included energy and material sources for EVs, using EVs as storage for the electric grid, and EV recommendations. pages.text: 24 Wednesday, March 15, 2023 Regenerative Gala to Spotlight Ethical Consumerism To kick off Earth Month on April 1, a Bay Area event called the Regenerative Gala will promote the concepts of ethical consumerism and fashion and art as a vehicle for change. The event’s fashion show rejects so-called “fast fashion” which produces clothes in sweatshops, often made from petroleum-based synthetic fabrics. Joelle Provost, a low-impact painter whose works will be featured, said the focus is on natural fabrics produced on farms avoiding pesticides, rejuvenating the soil, and paying a living wage. “A lot of small brands are saying, let’s source our textiles from the farmers so that we know that the ecosystems are being supported on those small farms,” Provost explained. “It’s all about small-batch fabrics.” The gala takes place on Saturday, April 1, at 6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, in Piedmont. Tickets are $150–$300 and available online at https://www. eventbrite.com/e/410109317007. An art auction will feature works promoting a healthy environment and the fight against climate change. To explore the auction and register to bid remotely, go to https://givebutter.com/c/ GnyZu0/auction. Julian Adon Alexander, The Regenerative Gala will feature a runway with models wearing fashions made of natural fabrics produced on farms. another featured artist, will offer paintings raising awareness about the lack of green space in urban neighborhoods of color. “I just think exposure to new ideas is really the point of art,” Alexander noted. “I don’t think it necessarily solves problems, it just introduces something into somebody’s mind.” Food & wine The Gala will feature a chef that works closely with local USDA organic farmers and is committed to minimal packaging. Also featured are wines from a permaculture vineyard in Sonoma County. The Gala will emphasize low-waste, local products to inspire people to use their lifestyle and purchasing power to live in harmony with the earth rather than plunder its natural resources. Proceeds will benefit the Agrarian Trust, a nonprofit supporting land access for the next generation of farmers. LWV discussion in Piedmont on electric vehicles By Jennifer Trainor Dr. Daniel Sperling, the Distinguished Blue Planet Prize Professor of Civil Engineering and Environmental Science and Policy and founding Director of the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California in Davis, was the guest speaker on March 1 in Piedmont. His discussion was sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Dr. Sperling described renewable electricity generation and EV usage as the #1 and #2 solutions to climate damage. The shift to EVs is already underway with EVs representing 13% of passenger car sales worldwide in 2022. China and the E.U. lead EV passenger sales with approximately 54% and 29% of global unit sales respectively. The U.S. is a distant 3rd place with less than 12% of passenger EV unit sales. Among U.S. states, California is a front-runner in the transition to EVs. Currently, 20% of California’s passenger car sales are EVs – good news for local air quality and public health. Dr. Sperling has kept California in the vanguard of climate leadership in the transportation sector. For the past 16 years, he has held the Transportation seat on the California Air Resources Board (CARB), which adopted its first EV rules in 1990. EV adoption is scheduled to accelerate in California with CARB regulations mandating that EVs reach 33% of passenger car sales by 2026, 66% by 2030 and 100% by 2035. New buses will have to be 100% ZEV (Zero-Emission Vehicles) by 2029 and even new long-haul trucks will be ZEV by 2035. Enabling this rapid transition has been the precipitous decline in battery prices which have decreased 90% in real dollars, from approximately $1,200/ kWh in 2010 to roughly $100/ kWh today. Dr. Sperling shared some mild uncertainties about the pace of EV adoption including fluctuations in battery costs, lags in domestic battery materials supplies, processing, and manufacturing, and slower development of public charging infrastructure, especially to support long-haul road transportation. He is convinced by historical precedents that public and private investment will generate market solutions to surmount these hurdles. In addition to EVs, Dr. Sperling discussed the benefits of, and use-case scenarios for, hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles. He said that hydrogen fuel cells are likely to be important for larger vehicles such as buses and long-haul transportation needs, or for people living in very cold climates who have very long daily commutes. Dr. Sperling closed the session by taking questions from the audience. When asked about housing policy and public transit as means of reducing vehicle-miles-traveled, Dr. Sperling emphasized that reducing vehicle use is a winning strategy that is worthy of public investment. To illustrate this point, he cited the example of his home city of Davis where urban planners and city leaders gradually built a network of safe bike paths widely used by riders of all ages. He said that bikes now account for 30-40% of work trips in Davis. In addition to developing safe biking infrastructure, especially to connect the “last mile” of homes and businesses to public transit, he sees shared, autonomous transportation-on-demand as a promising solution for reducing vehicle-use and for providing convenient and affordable public transportation using larger cars or vans. He notes 3 companies who are currently testing this technology on a limited basis in the Bay Area. Additional question topics included energy and material sources for EVs, using EVs as storage for the electric grid, and EV recommendations. Recycling Tips By Sophie Roberts • Make sure your recyclables are empty, clean, dry The City of Piedmont has “single stream” recycling where all recyclable materials are put into one bin and eventually separated at a facility in Richmond. If recyclable materials haven’t been rinsed or cleaned out ahead of time, it can cause a mess. Paper is especially vulnerable to grease and moisture. One half-full soda can or greasy takeout container can contaminate the other recyclables in the bin, turning them into trash. • Don’t be an “aspirational” recycler Have you ever put an item in the recycling bin because you thought it should be recyclable? This phenomenon is known as aspirational recycling or “wishcycling.” Such materials include single-use utensils and straws, plastic bags, chip bags, and waxed cartons. Often, wishcycling contaminates recyclables and causes whole batches of recyclable loads to be thrown away. Remember: When in doubt, throw it out. • Don’t include e-waste E-waste can be recycled, but it doesn’t belong in the blue bin. Batteries can be dropped off at the Fire Department or can be placed in a sealed zip-lock plastic bag on top of your blue recycling cart on your regular collection day. For other e-waste items, call Republic Services at 800-320-8077 to schedule a curbside pickup. • If it’s smaller than a credit card, it belongs in the trash Small items like clothing tags, bottle caps, straws, and scraps of paper can clog machinery and are unlikely to be recycled. Recycling loads are delivered to Richmond where they are unloaded and put on conveyor belts for mechanical removal of aluminum cans, plastics and glass. The remaining materials are hand-sorted to recover cardboard and other reusable material as possible. • Don’t bag your recyclables Plastic bags can clog recycling equipment, which may lead sorting facilities to throw away your bagged recyclables. By omitting the bag, you’re creating less waste. • Reduce and reuse before you recycle Did you know that the three R’s are in that order for a reason? Recycling should be a last resort, after reducing and reusing. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov. The group was pleased to welcome Alissa Quan, Ken Moy, Leonore Deaton, Dale Breen, and Steve Canine with K-9 best friend Mochie who were with the group for the first time. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had another big crowd of 50 walkers and a kennel of K-9 best friends last week. Besides the good weather there was another reason for the large turnout. A special destination was planned. Some of the walkers remembered in 2021 when they visited a home on Littlewood Drive with a truly unique yard, the site of of a historical former Silk Farm. They went down the cul-de-sac to its end where there is a private driveway that continues to a red London phone booth in front of a home’s gates. owner Laura Plitkins was coming out and invited the walkers to come see the “tropical oasis” she and her husband, Michael, had created. Walkers Swee Ling and Albert Chen are her neighbors and told her how much the group had enjoyed their first visit The house is going on the market in April, so the group knew it needed to schedule a visit before then. The walkers made the first climb up Mountain Avenue. They passed the stately former home of U.S. Senator William Knowland on Sea View Avenue and continued on to Dudley Avenue, passing beautiful tulip magnolias in full bloom, to the top of Littlewood. They regrouped there to hear Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. They planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are food for silk worms. Unfortunately, the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese silk workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. The group descended Littlewood’s canyon where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees were once planted. At the end of the street Laura Plitkins was there to greet the walkers, and led them down their long, steep driveway to the side of their house and pool, guarded by a large statue of a dinosaur. Michael was waiting for the group and told them the house is one of six homes built on land that was once owned by the daughter of Domingo Ghirardelli, founder of the Ghirardelli Chocolate Company. The Plitkins bought the house in 2014. Michael has a company that creates unique structures and virtual soundscapes. Over five and a half years the Plitkins transformed the area at the house’s front into an incredible tropical garden with a pool, water slide, and pool house. Jungle sound effects enhance the other-world imaginary. Michael encouraged the group to walk below the pool on a stone path where they found replica Mayan tablets, bamboo and palm trees, and a natural creek running alongside. The walkers emerged near the pool house where Laura had coffee and pastries waiting for them. The group talked with Michael and Laura for some time before taking a group photo by the pool. All too soon it was time to retrace their steps back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.
