articles.text: During its meeting on Monday, March 13 the Piedmont Planning Commission received an update on the city’s response to the state on its Housing Element. Planning staff will bring the Element and its Initial Study-Negative Declaration (ISND) to City Council, to be considered for adoption, next Monday, March 20. On the whole, Jackson emphasized, the comments by California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) reviewers don’t “requir[e] a structural change to the Element, such as a change in the sites identified in the inventory.” The Element and HCD review are available at PiedmontIsHome.org. On Friday, March 17, the revised Element will be posted on piedmont.ca.gov and PiedmontIsHome.org, as part of the agenda packet for the Monday, March 20 City Council meeting. After the Element is posted, said Jackson, “there will be seven days where the public can submit comments before we can send [the Element] off to HCD for a second review, and that generally lasts 60 days, which would put us at the end of May.” Among the additions requested in the HCD comments were a discussion of the “effectiveness of the previous Housing Element’s programs to address the housing needs of special needs populations”; “how the city proactively complies with fair housing laws and regulations”; and how the Element sites are expected to “improve and/or exacerbate fair housing conditions.” Much of the additional analysis requested regarded the needs of lower-income and special needs populations. For example, the city’s definition of a family as applied to zoning use “appears to have potential constraints on persons with disabilities such as requiring families to be ‘traditional,’ ‘sharing household activities’ and requiring a ‘single written lease.’” “While the Element identifies the total number of households overpaying for housing,” reviewers requested that the city quantify “the number of lower-income households overpaying for housing,” he added. Reviewers also asked that the Element demonstrate that the city’s existing and planned water and sewer infrastructure can accommodate planned housing without any overload. The city’s presentation included research showing Piedmont’s compliance with fair housing laws; proof of water and sewer capacity to accommodate new housing; how Piedmont’s housing programs impact economic and housing mobility for low-income and special needs populations; and recent rental and sale prices in Piedmont. Many comments referenced the fact that Piedmont’s Housing Element relies on non-vacant sites to accommodate over 50% of its lower-income housing, and the fact that “a large portion” of these “lower-income [sites] is isolated in three remote areas on the boundaries of the city yet a significant portion of the moderate and above moderate [sites] is located throughout the city.” The city’s approach is to show the travel times to schools, parks, and Civic Center from these areas, and demonstrate the fact that “Piedmont is a neighborhood-size small city … that access to amenities does not stop at the City boundary, that amenities in Oakland are generally [accessible] within a reasonable walking distance.” Furthermore, Jackson emphasized that unmapped sites like future ADUs and some sites like Moraga Canyon would “add units of all income types” throughout Piedmont. As part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. Completing this requirement, the IS-ND determined that the Housing Element as a document will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For example, the city’s definition of a family as applied to zoning use “appears to have potential constraints on persons with disabilities such as requiring families to be ‘traditional,’ ‘sharing household activities’ and requiring a ‘single written lease.’” “While the Element identifies the total number of households overpaying for housing,” reviewers requested that the city quantify “the number of lower-income households overpaying for housing,” he added. Reviewers also asked that the Element demonstrate that the city’s existing and planned water and sewer infrastructure can accommodate planned housing without any overload. The city’s presentation included research showing Piedmont’s compliance with fair housing laws; proof of water and sewer capacity to accommodate new housing; how Piedmont’s housing programs impact economic and housing mobility for low-income and special needs populations; and recent rental and sale prices in Piedmont. Many comments referenced the fact that Piedmont’s Housing Element relies on non-vacant sites to accommodate over 50% of its lower-income housing, and the fact that “a large portion” of these “lower-income [sites] is isolated in three remote areas on the boundaries of the city yet a significant portion of the moderate and above moderate [sites] is located throughout the city.” The city’s approach is to show the travel times to schools, parks, and Civic Center from these areas, and demonstrate the fact that “Piedmont is a neighborhood-size small city … that access to amenities does not stop at the City boundary, that amenities in Oakland are generally [accessible] within a reasonable walking distance.” Furthermore, Jackson emphasized that unmapped sites like future ADUs and some sites like Moraga Canyon would “add units of all income types” throughout Piedmont. As part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. Completing this requirement, the IS-ND determined that the Housing Element as a document will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome. org.
